analysis.one_liner: Repeals Medicare drug price negotiation, inflation rebates, and the out-of-pocket cost cap.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the Senate Finance Committee, and the Inflation Reduction Act's drug price provisions remain in effect.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe out the three main prescription drug provisions of the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022: Medicare's new power to negotiate the prices of certain expensive drugs, a rule forcing drug makers to pay rebates when their prices rise faster than inflation, and the cap limiting what Medicare beneficiaries pay out of pocket each year. It was introduced by two Senate Republicans and referred to the Finance Committee, which took no further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Brand-name drug manufacturers gain the most: they would no longer face Medicare-negotiated prices, would stop paying rebates when prices outpace inflation, and could charge Medicare patients higher prices up front. Supporters argue this would protect investment in future drug research.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals, retroactive to enactment, the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program, meaning Medicare would return to paying whatever prices drug companies set rather than negotiated maximums.
It removes the requirement that drug manufacturers pay rebates to Medicare when a drug's price rises faster than inflation, freeing companies from that penalty.
It eliminates the annual out-of-pocket spending cap under the Medicare drug benefit, which had limited how much beneficiaries must pay each year for prescriptions.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers. Seniors would lose the $2,000-style annual cap on drug costs, and Medicare would pay more for drugs whose prices had been negotiated or held down by inflation rebates — costs that flow back to patients through premiums and cost-sharing.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the inflation rebate and price negotiation would remove the main checks on drug prices in Medicare, shifting more of the cost onto beneficiaries and the federal budget.

The bill would have no offsetting savings; the CRS summary describes only repeals, so the federal government would lose the revenue from negotiated prices and manufacturer rebates without replacing it.

The strongest good-faith objection in its favor: supporters contend that government price-setting and inflation penalties could reduce investment in new medicines, which is the argument behind the bill's name.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's entire effect is to undo drug price limits enacted in 2022. The savings to drug companies are concrete and immediate — higher prices on existing Medicare drugs — while the promised benefit of future innovation is indirect and speculative. For the tens of millions of people on Medicare, the bill's passage would have meant losing the out-of-pocket cap and the lower negotiated prices, with no new protection in exchange.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee in June 2023, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Lee introduced the bill on June 22, 2023, with Sen. Marco Rubio as its sole cosponsor.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day, which was the last action of any kind on the bill.
The bill targeted the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program, the inflation-rebate requirement, and the annual out-of-pocket cap created by the Inflation Reduction Act.
Because the Congress ended in January 2025 without the Finance Committee holding a hearing, markup, or vote, the drug price provisions the bill sought to repeal remain in effect.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers are better off because the bill died: they keep the negotiated drug prices, the inflation-rebate protection, and the annual out-of-pocket cap. Brand-name drug makers, who stood to regain pricing power worth billions, did not get it back.

for.name: Sen. Mike Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Inflation Reduction Act's drug price provisions.

for.name: Pharmaceutical research and manufacturing industry
for.role: Industry opposed to the IRA drug provisions
for.what_they_did: Publicly campaigned against the Inflation Reduction Act's Medicare drug price negotiation and inflation rebate provisions and supported their repeal.

against.name: Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; the committee's only recorded action was the referral, and no vote ever occurred.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by two Senate Republicans and drew no Democratic cosponsors; no vote was ever held, so the only recorded support was partisan.

industries.note: Repeal would free these companies from Medicare-negotiated prices, inflation-based rebates, and the out-of-pocket cap that limits what patients pay — restoring their ability to set prices for drugs sold to Medicare. Their gain comes directly out of higher costs for beneficiaries and the federal government.
